title: JSON vs SQL

drills.q: An order has 1–20 line items, always shown together with the order, owned by it, and never queried independently. Where should the line items live?
options: In a separate table joined at read time
Embedded in the order's JSONB document, giving one lookup per order
drills.explain: The items are bounded, owned and read together, so embedding gives better locality with no loss. Keep order id, customer id and status as real columns for querying.

drills.q: A social app stores each user's follower list inside the user's JSONB document. One celebrity has 40 million followers. What is the problem, and what is the fix?
options: The document grows without bound, so each read and update touches a huge value and nearly every follow rewrites it; model followers as a separate relation (a table of user_id, follower_id)
The follower list should be put in an HTTP header
drills.explain: Embedding assumes bounded, parent-owned data. An unbounded relationship is the signature case for normalization (or a dedicated store), and it also needs to be queried from the other side ('who does X follow').

drills.q: A product name is embedded in 40,000 order documents of about 4 KB each. When the name is corrected, you decide to update every order. Assuming each update rewrites the whole document, how much data is rewritten, in MB (1 MB = 1000 KB)?
drills.explain: 40,000 × 4 KB = 160,000 KB = 160 MB, plus index and WAL overhead. In a normalized model one row in `products` changes. For orders the right answer is usually to keep the old name (a snapshot), which is why embedding historical facts is acceptable but embedding mutable shared facts is costly.

drills.q: Which are real costs of storing data as JSONB instead of columns? Select all that apply.
options: Fields inside the document cannot have foreign keys or NOT NULL enforced by the database
A one-field change typically rewrites the whole document value
Aggregations across documents (e.g. revenue per category) are slower and more awkward than on indexed columns
A single lookup can no longer return multiple related items
drills.explain: The last statement is backwards: returning related items in one lookup is the benefit. The other three are the reasons shared, constrained or analysed fields stay relational.

drills.q: Explain the JSONB-vs-SQL decision in terms of data locality, with one case for each side.
drills.answer: Embedding related data in one JSONB document puts everything one read needs in one place (one lookup instead of several queries/joins). Use it for bounded, parent-owned, read-together data like order line items. Use normalized tables for shared, unbounded or independently updated data like products, followers or events, and for anything needing constraints or cross-row aggregation.
